speechtext: Mr. Chairman, under this vote I assume it will be in order to discuss matters relating to the penitentiaries.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe a discussion of penitentiaries would be more properly debatable under item 96 of the estimates.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I could discuss the matter of the policy of the department under this item. Hon. members who sat in parliament between 1930 and 1935, and more especially those who sat between 1935 and 1940, will recall that largely as a result of the agitation.-I was almost going to say misplaced activities-of the former hon. member for Grey-Bruce, and as a result of the newspaper agitation of the Toronto Globe as constituted in earlier days, five years ago to-day this government set up another royal commission to investigate our whole penal system.
The commission consisted of Mr. Justice Joseph Archambault, of the superior court of the province of Quebec, a distinguished former member of this house, one whom it was always a pleasure to know and to meet, and who had had a wide experience at the bar in criminal practice ; Mr. R. W. Craig, K.C. of Winnipeg, at one time I believe attorney general for Manitoba, and Mr. Harry W. Anderson, a distinguished member of the press gallery, in his lifetime a noted publicist in Canada, one who had taken a keen personal interest in the matter and had been to a great extent if not wholly responsible for the attitude of the Globe at that time. Unfortunately Mr. Anderson passed away, and his place was taken by Mr. McRuer, an experienced lawyer

Supply-Justice
of Toronto-and,- by the way, a defeated Liberal candidate in the constituency of High Park.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: One of the few.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Was a Liberal candidate defeated? He must have been a rare specimen.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: A rara avis?-there are such in this world, and there will be more later.
They are not rare in Toronto.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
However, that is by the way. This commission made an exhaustive survey. They held sittings in every province; they went to all the principal centres across the dominion. They held sittings in my own city. In 1937 they visited the United States. They went overseas to study the penal systems of England, Scotland, Holland, Belgium, Germany and France. On April 4, 1938-almost three years ago-the commission presented to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) a report consisting of 418 pages. The cost of that commission to the taxpayers of Canada was, I am told, $88,810.25.
The recommendations of the commission were numerous and varied. They were so varied in fact that I shall not take up the time of the house to dwell upon them. That is not the point I have in mind. One of the recommendations which appealed strongly to the government was that a commission system should be established to administer our penitentiary system in Canada, rather than have it carried on under administration by the department, through a superintendent.
Late in the session of 1938, almost I believe in the dying days of that session, the Minister of Justice brought to the house a bill providing for the appointment of a penitentiaries commission, but carrying into effect very few of the remaining recommendations made by the royal commission. If I remember correctly, that bill, and its successor, which was subsequently enacted, reenacted a large number of the provisions of the act found in the revised statutes of Canada. The principal departure was the setting up of the principle of commission administration, in contradistinction to departmental administration. I was not then in parliament, but I understand vigorous protests were made by the opposition to the effect that sufficient opportunity was not given at that time, in the dying days of the session, properly to consider the matter.
The Minister of Justice, however, insisted on the passage of the bill, and on June 29, 1938, he made this statement, as reported at page 43S3 of Hansard-I direct particular attention to the passage I quote:
It is a necessity, because I do not see how we can proceed under the present system after what has taken place. I would not feel that I could safely be responsible for the administration of the penitentiaries.
That .is to say, he would not feel he could be responsible if the system was continued under the old law. I pause here to say that due largely to economic conditions in Canada beginning, we will say, in 1929 and continuing on until very recent years, there was a substantial increase in the criminal population of our penitentiaries. Most of this increase was due to economic stress; most of the cases were cases of robbery and robbery with violence, and a very considerable number of desperate characters were incarcerated in our penal institutions during that period. Among them were some communists, about whom we have heard this afternoon. They carried on their nefarious work among the criminal population with the result that there were riots and all that sort of thing, an aspect of the matter which at the moment I need not traverse. But I want to emphasize the fact that it was probably because of the situation then existing that the minister made the statement which I have quoted.
The minister having made that statement upon his responsibility as the directing head of the penitentiary system, the then leader of the opposition waived his objection to the bill and it passed this house. Subsequently- I think for the same reason that had been alleged in this house, and possibly others- the bill was rejected in the other house, and there the matter stood. When the Minister of Justice announced to the house the rejection of the bill in the senate he made this statement, which will be found at page 4511 of Hansard of June 30, 1938:
All I may add is that this postponement of a needed reform, apart from being detrimental to public interest, and increasing to a dangerous degree the difficulties of my task, will not serve any useful purpose, not even that which seems to be at the basis of the adverse vote.
He was referring, of course, to the action of the other house.
In the following session the minister presented the same bill, and it passed both houses and received the royal assent on April
5,	1939, nearly two years ago. The act is cited as The Penitentiary Act, 1939, chapter
6.	3 George VI, the last section of which, section 84, provides that the act shall come into force on a date to be fixed by proclama-
Supply-Justice

tion of the governor in council published in the Canada Gazette. I have had search made in the Canada Gazette, and I find that this statute has never been proclaimed. In view of the minister's statements to which I have referred, and which obviously were made in good faith-I am not suggesting anything else -one would have expected immediate action- the proclamation of the bill and the appointment of a commission to relieve the minister of the responsibility which he found so onerous and indeed dangerous. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, this was not in war time.
As I have stated, the main purpose of the bill was to set up a commission form of administration for our penal institutions, a three-man commission instead of a one-man superintendency.
What is the situation to-day? Two years have gone by. The bill has not been proclaimed, no appointments have been made, the minister still bears the heavy and onerous and dangerous burden-and in addition there is a war on. One of the inspectors continues to act as superintendent, and apparently with satisfaction, because we do not hear a word about him. If the former member for Grey-Bruce were in the house we might be hearing something about the penitentiaries, but that element having been removed from our society the agitation has entirely ceased. I am not saying that in any derogatory sense at all. She apparently has accomplished her mission here in this reform of our penal institutions and is no doubt devoting her attention to other activities, with profit I hope to herself and to those with whom she is associated. The minister is still carrying on under the old system, and I think he is to be congratulated. The cost of the superintendency to-day is less than $5,000 for salary. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I think I am right. The acting superintendent has the standing of an inspector with the pay of that position.
Under the proposed set-up a three-man commission is to be appointed, costing this country $24,000 a year, with a chairman at $9,000 and two other commissioners at $7,500 a year. The time has arrived when the minister ought to abandon this whole proposal, scrap the bill, appoint a superintendent of penitentiaries and proceed under the old act, which is to be found in the revised statutes.
I suggest that never at any time was this proposal anything more than a sop to the former member for Grey-Bruce and to certain newspapers. In view of the fact that our penal system has operated with apparent success on the old basis, and especially so during the past two or three years, I suggest that the proposed commission be relegated to the same pigeon-

hole as that in which most of the other recommendations of the $88,000 royal commission are to be found. The major part of them will never emerge and see the light of day.
By the way, if hon. gentlemen will look at the estimates they will see that this money has been voted each year since the passing of the act, and it is in the estimates to-day; but the statute itself has never been proclaimed and the money is not spent. Let us do away with this farce. Let us proceed under a system that is reasonably satisfactory, and, I would add, much more economical to the taxpayers of Canada in this time of war. I invite the minister to take heed of the suggestions I have made to him. The present is no time to embark on these new expenditures. I urge upon the minister that he remove these votes from the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The
leader of the opposition has been fairly accurate in the historical review he has given of this matter, except in some particulars, and he adorned his oration with some comments, of course, that may not have been altogether called for. When the investigation commission was appointed there had been requests for it from various parts of Canada. My hon. friend gives too much credit to the former member for Grey-Bruce-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -when he states that she was the one responsible for the appointment of the commission. No doubt she was strongly in favour of it, but that attitude was not confined to the former member for Grey-Bruce. There had been difficulties and troubles, and the press had been commenting on our system in a not altogether favourable way. I remember that my own fellow townsman, Archdeacon Scott, the old padre, whom everybody in Canada loves, was perhaps the strongest advocate of a thorough investigation of our penitentiaries. As a matter of fact, in 1935 the present Prime Minister made it part of his platform; it w'as a pledge which he took before the electors of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Another
broken pledge?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He pledged there would be a commission to investigate the system.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
He was
safe.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
A commission, a very good one, as my hon. friend himself said, was appointed, and it did a

Supply-Justice
very fine piece of work. The reports of the commission deserve to be not only read but seriously studied by all those who are interested in social work. My hon. friend says that no part of the recommendations has been applied. Such of the recommendations as could be applied without the appointment of a commission, have been put into effect by regulation. As my hon. friend said, the bill was rejected by the senate in 1938. It was made law in 1939 at the end of the session, probably June.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: April.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
April?
Very well. Of course the main provision of the act is for the appointment of a permanent penitentiaries commission. My hon. friend said we should discard that altogether. May I remind him of what is stated in that report, that Canada is about the only country in the world where there is no commission in charge of prisons and penitentiaries. The British system has been mentioned in the house time and again; in Great Britain there is a very, very valuable commission. The United States and the various countries of Europe have commissions, and I believe that Canada should follow suit in this respect. Then, my hon. friend says, why do you not appoint the commission and why do you not proclaim the act? The act will be proclaimed when we are ready to appoint the commission. We could not proclaim the act without appointing the commission immediately.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Have there been any refusals to take these jobs?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No refusals, no. But I do not want to consider very much too-pressing applications for appointments to the commission. I think rather that we are trying to find the men without the men offering themselves for the work.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister will find plenty of men who want the jobs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend will say that the war is made responsible for all sorts of things, but I tell him in all sincerity that the war has something to do with this matter. At least a couple of men whom I had in mind for appointments on the commission are actually doing war work.
Any ladies?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. I have not thought about that, but if my hon. friend is making a serious suggestion, perhaps I may consider it.
I was just asking a question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No; I myself have not thought about it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That suggestion is settled, then, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will agree with me that it is better not to appoint the commission now than to have members who would not be qualified' for the work.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If you are going on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I can find suitable men for the job, even during the war, the commission will be appointed. That is the reason why I am still putting the item in the estimates. Unless, however, we are satisfied that we have the proper men to act on the commission, it is better to wait until our man power is not so much in demand as it is to-day. That is the only reason which has prevented the appointment of the commission. But I cannot accept the suggestion of my hon. friend and do away altogether with the proposal.

I should like to ask the minister a question in connection with this matter. I understand that there is a separate vote for penitentiaries, and probably I can say what I have to say on that particular subject when we reach that item. Is there not some way whereby the minister's department can be consolidated? No living man could stand the strain of the department as it is set up and constituted to-day. The minister is carrying on all the work which in England is divided among three departments. There, the Home Secretary has charge of the institutions referred to by my leader. Another, the Lord Chancellor has charge of the Law Courts, and another department relates to the office of the Attorney General. Three separate ministers divide the work. In Canada the Minister of Justice is not only Minister of Justice, but also Attorney General of Canada; he is the chief law officer of the crown and home secretary in Canada; that is his second function. His third function is Minister of Justice, which means that he is administrative officer of all justice in the country. He appoints the superior and county court judges. In England they have been discussing a report of a committee of the House of Commons to create a department of justice to handle all these matters, and a book by R. M. Jackson, on the machinery
Supply-Justice

of justice in England, which book came out last month and is in the library, deals with this problem.
In the present situation in Canada the Minister of Justice has not any time to attend to one of the main questions which Canada has to consider, relative to four unsolved problems- constitutional, cabinet, law and parliamentary reform, long overdue in this country and only talked about. I say the minister has no time whatever to attend to that, and one cannot expect him to do it. I wonder how, even with his fine ability, he has stood the strain as well as he has.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Thank you.

I would, however, suggest to him that during the parliamentary recess some consideration should be given to the important subject of law, cabinet, parliamentary and constitutional reform in Canada, because we are away behind the times. Al-thought the present minister may know much more about the matter than I do, I believe he, as head, could divide this burden with others. There should be one minister responsible solely for the administration of justice in all four items but with more help. The present minister should be assisted by an attorney general, who would appear in the law courts and undertake duties of that sort. Then, the kind of work performed by the department of the Home Secretary in England has become in Canada a very large and important part of the Department of Justice with its large detail of administration. We have had a report on this matter by a very good commission on prison reform, but the report has not yet been consummated. That part of the report about the Borstal system should be dealt with, and a great part of the recommendations contained in the report should be carried out at once, war or no war.
At the present time the administration of the department must necessarily devolve upon deputies who should get reforms under way. The head of the department, the minister, who visits various places and appoints staff has considerable work to do unless he has ample assistance. I suggest that in the recess the minister should endeavour to bring about some form of consolidation whereby deputies or other ministers might be appointed to take care of the various aspects of the work of the department.
One matter I would mention in connection with the branch of the department that has jurisdiction over law reform is the appointment of judges. More care should be taken. Many judges to-day leave the bench for

months and even for a year or two, to engage in commission work in the provinces. This runs into large sums of money, and their judicial duties have to be carried out by others. I had a bill before the house a few years ago to provide that any judge who might be appointed on any commission, political or otherwise, should first vacate his judgeship. While they are on such work, away from their judicial duties, others must take their place, and work becomes congested because a salary is provided in the estimates for each of them.
With regard to the report to which I have already referred respecting machinery of government, laid before the British House of Commons and the House of Lords, the appointment of judges would be transferred to the Lord Chancellor who would have power to consult a committee, including the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and others.
I suggest that something should be done to relieve the congestion that exists in the courts as a result of the absence of judges from sickness and other causes-and there is at times considerable congestion in some provinces.
The chief constables' association has laid many matters before the government. For one thing it has proposed the abolition of air rifles. On a street car the other day on Bathurst street a woman was sitting near a window when a shot from an air gun came through the window and struck her, nearly blinding one eye and it might have blinded the other had her head been turned that way. I hope the government will adopt the recommendation of the association in this regard and prevent the manufacture of air guns and ban them.
Different bills have been introduced into this house having for their purpose various amendments to the criminal code in order to bring about much needed improvements in motor vehicular traffic. I hope that the minister will seriously consider adopting some of these proposals and that some definite action will be taken during the recess. I do not wish to see any member of this house knocked down by any hit-and-run driver. There is an awful slaughter on the highways to-day. I hope that the department will broaden its functions to provide some remedy for the present situation, because the slaughter is almost as bad as the destruction of life in war. Every roadway is turned red, and the loss of life is deplorable and one of Canada's scandals.
The rule has been laid down that the Attorney General of Canada should not be asked to offer legal opinions in the house, and I commend the present minister for his observance of that rule. I only regret that

Supply-Justice
the attorneys general of some of our provinces, instead of adopting a similar attitude, have seen fit to give a great many opinions on various matters. The subject matters may come before the law courts and the attorneys general are judicial officers.
Another amendment which I should like to see the department introduce is with regard to juries, to provide, for instance, that the judge shall enter verdict without any comment, because the functions of the judge and the jury are clearly defined. I trust that the jury system will not be interfered with in the code, because it has done good work and is badly needed at the present time.
Another matter to which I might refer is the question of appeals to the privy council. The former member for St. Lawrence-St. George had a bill before this house for the abolition of such appeals, and the matter went to the supreme court. I hope the bill will be left in abeyance. Appeals to the privy council are one link we hold within the empire. Under the Supreme Court Act I should like to see a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada of a bill I introduced to provide that the judges in this country shall follow the decisions of his majesty in his privy council. The case on marriage laws here came up and a decision was given on validity. This has been supported by Chief Justice Greenshields of Quebec, a very able judge, who laid down that they are legal and no canon law should upset them, I have no doubt that if there were an appeal on a question of law to the Supreme Court of Canada under the Supreme Court Act, they would establish the decision of Mr. Justice Greenshields as the law of this country long overdue. The courts are subservient to the legislature, and it is the duty of judges to interpret the law as it stands, as it is found in the textbooks and the authorities and by the court of last resort, the privy council, one court where a litigant is always sure of substantial justice. I submit that the department should come to some decision in this matter. Many requests have been made to have such an appeal taken. The minister, after all, has a function to perform as Attorney General to enforce the law and clear up the law.
In passing, may I request the right hon. gentleman's attention for a moment as Minister of Justice. I see the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) in conversation with him. I do not like to interrupt them, but I suggest that the subject I am discussing at the moment is of sufficient importance to call for a little of the minister's undivided attention for a few minutes. Yesterday, humorously he was talking about some of the
"N.G.s" on this side. I was not one selected for the minister's team by him of the "N.G.s" "N.G." means "no game," "no goal," "no guts," "no girl," no anything you like. I hope my good friend the hon. member for Parkdale did not go over to get on the Minister of Justice team to tell him what "N.G." means, and how to play if he gets on the team, because the minister has a keen sense of good humour.
I would ask in all seriousness that the minister state a case to be referred to the supreme court in order to determine that question of law, that judges shall follow the decisions of his majesty in his privy council, because the decisions of the privy council in London are binding on all the courts of this country in every province.
I have already referred to the question of motor car accidents, but the situation to-day is so serious that I refer to it once again by way of emphasis. I hope the minister will seriously consider an amendment that will give us a real remedy. Why, fifty-four soldiers, some by hit-and-run drivers, have been knocked down and killed in the various military districts in one year. I do not want to see the minister himself knocked down, but I know he has been in danger himself. I saw him walking in front of the Rideau club one day and he had a close shave. He may not have seen the car of which he might easily have been a victim. I should not like to see the hon. member for Parkdale or the Prime Minister, or the leader of the opposition or the learned Minister of Pensions run any risks, because they do not step as lively as they used to, nor do any of us sometimes.
It is impossible for the Minister of Justice efficiently to discharge his duties unless he is given additional help along the lines I have suggested, namely, on the judicial and the administrative sides and in connection with work similar to that done in England by the Home Secretary.
Many recommendations have been made with regard to amendments to the code, and I do hope that something will be done to implement some of the most urgent of them. I think the minister is to be commended for bringing down his estimates so early in the session, so that judges and others in authority may have an opportunity to express themselves with regard to any statutory amendments that may be contemplated. The department is a very good one; there is an active minister, and I hope that during the recess he will take these suggestions into consideration.
Canada is away behind the times in law reform. It has been talked of for twenty-
Supply-Justice

five years. They have accomplished it in England; as a result of the Summary Offenders Act they closed up half the prisons in England. In Canada, law reform is discussed only by the bar at its conventions, but it should be the most important work of this house in committee.

I should like to ask the minister a question, following what my leader said in reference to the report upon which the minister had made suggestions a few years ago. At that time there was a good deal of talk about instituting in the penitentiaries of Canada some means of reform along the lines of the Borstal system that has shown such splendid results in England.
In speaking on the question a few years ago, I referred to my own survey of the penitentiaries of England and the fine things I saw as a result of that system. Has anything along that line been incorporated in the administration of the Canadian penitentiaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This was one of the important matters that were left for the consideration of the commission when appointed, and that is the reason why really nothing has been done. If we ever come to the conclusion that no commission should be appointed, this matter will have to be considered. But I still hope to give effect to the recommendations of the report and have the commission appointed, and that system which my hon. friend has discussed in the house on some occasions and of which I know personally he has made a special study, put into effect as far as possible.

I should like to suggest
publicly, as I was doing privately to the Minister of Justice, that this matter of appointing commissioners, involving considerable expenditure, might very well be left over until after the war.
Second, may I say that I personally have had some experience in making a report, and although in my case the report was not approved publicly, twenty-four of my recommendations out of twenty-five were put into effect. I think, therefore, that the Minister of Justice could very well implement many of the recommendations of the report even in advance of the appointment of the commissioners.

I cannot support that point of view at all. It seems to me an oversimplification to say that the bill setting up the penitentiaries commission was purely a sop to the former member for Grey-Bruce. It is true that the former member

for Grey-Bruce and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) were both enthusiastic advocates of penitentiary reform. But there were hundreds of people, penologists and others interested in the penal problem in Canada, who for years had been pressing upon the government, both the former government and this one, the need for setting up a commission to institute modern methods of dealing with people who had broken the law and were in need of a new adaptation to society. We in this group were most enthusiastic when the government finally did bring down the bill to set up this commission. Whether there is a war on or not, this country can fight it efficiently and vigorously only as it has behind it a solidified state, and at the core of any state there lies its judiciary and its method of dealing with the malcontent and people who have broken the laws and have come under the punishment of the state.
No one has suggested that, as a war measure, we should reduce this huge sum being paid to judges, over $2,000,000, or the $300,000 being paid in pensions. If we are going to take care of one end of the law, we must also take care of the other. If we are going to spend money to try men and put them away where they can do no harm, we must also be prepared for the sake of the state to take care of these men when they come out of prison, and help them to make a proper adaptation, get back into society and play a part in the Canada that is to be w-hen this war is over.
Someone suggested $24,000 for salaries alone for the commission. That sum or ten times that sum, if necessary for administration and so on, will be a small amount compared with what we may pay for failing to do something about penal conditions in Canada.
I was very glad to hear the minister say that the government have no intention of discarding the bill and that they do intend to follow through with the appointment of the commission. I hope the minister will continue along that course; that it will not be long until the necessary men are found and the commission set up, so that something along the lines of the Borstal system as it has operated so successfully in England can be set up in Canada and we begin to do something for that section of our society which has been too long neglected and overlooked.

When this item of departmental administration was up for consideration in the 1940 session, I asked the Minister of lustice if he would give consideration to the appointment of a solicitor general, to be in ;harge particularly of the administration of

Supply-Justice
the defence of Canada regulations. At that time I pointed out, what the minister so clearly indicated this afternoon, that the administration of these regulations is based upon ministerial responsibility rather than judicial responsibility. It seemed to me then, and it does now, that it might be better if there were a minister of the crown whose sole or principal duty it would be to administer those regulations. Of course there are probably fewer cases now going through than there were last year, so the work is not so heavy. Has consideration been given to that suggestion, and, if so, has any decision been reached?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Consideration has certainly been given to the suggestion of my hon. friend. Of course that would mean an enlargement of the cabinet. Personally I think it is not absolutely essential that another man should be appointed to do this work. As my hon. friend says, the number of cases rather decreases because most of those who were under suspicion or to be interned have already come under the supervising control of the department. If, however, the work really justifies the course suggested by my hon. friend, I should be only too pleased to divide the work, but although I thank the hon. member for Broadview for his kind words and solicitude about my health, I am not as bad as I look.
With reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview, in England not three but four ministers do the work that is done by the Minister of Justice here. They include the Home Secretary, the Attorney General, the Solicitor General and the Lord Chancellor, who appoints the judges and is responsible for them. But we must not forget that in England they have not a federal system, while we have nine provinces, with nine attorneys general and nine departments concerned with the administration of justice, which certainly makes a difference in the work that has to be done by the Minister of Justice in Canada. I will, however, still consider the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver South.

I would not want the minister to take it that I was questioning his judgment in these cases; I do not think anyone in the house questions that. It is simply a question whether it is physically possible for the minister, with his many other duties, to review each of these cases in detail.
In connection with the internment camps I notice that the return filed by the minister some days ago covering internments under regulation 21 from November 1, 1940, to February 17, 1941, divides them into four classes; Germans, Italians, communists and National Unity party. I do not know whether the one from the National Unity party is exMayor Houde of Montreal, or under which classification he comes. Could the minister tell us how many people there are in internment camps at the moment, divided into these classes or in any other way he wishes, and also how many women have been interned? Last year I think only two women were interned, one German and one Italian. I should like to know how many are interned at the moment, and the class in which they come.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will
try to have that information when the resolution discussed earlier this afternoon comes up for further consideration. I must say, however, that after having laid on the table of the house the statement to which my hon. friend has just referred, I found that in it I had gone beyond the recommendations of the committee. I was requested only to give the number of internments and the number of cases in which the Minister of Justice had declined to accept the recommendations of the committees. I am not quite sure that it is in the public interest that the classification I gave should have been given. If, however, I can amplify what has been stated already, certainly I will do so. So far as the number of people interned is concerned, certainly that can be given, together with the number of women, and I will have that information available.

Could the minister tell us
whether or not any internees have been released without a recommendation on the part of the committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: None.

I have just one or two
observations to make in connection with these estimates. First, I should like to commend the Minister of Justice for having included in the estimates an appropriation to set up the penitentiaries commission. The criticism that this is a sop to the former member for Grey-Bruce is not well founded. By inference that means that it is a sop to a number of other people in this house and throughout the country who were interested in penitentiary reform. I am quite sure the leader of the opposition would not be quite so brave in the presence of the former member for Grey-Bruce as he has attempted to be this afternoon. After all, if the provisions of the Penitentiary Act, 1939, are implemented, the will of parliament will be carried out. That
Supply-Justice

act was placed upon, the statute books of this country by the representatives of the people, and if it is not implemented or if the government intimated that they did not intend to implement it, I am quite sure that there would be a storm of protest from one end of this country to the other, and that the agitation for penitentiary reform which was carried on prior to the enactment of this bill would start all over again.
The minister has said that men capable of carrying on such administration may not be immediately available. Be that as it may, however, there are, I am sure, plenty of other men capable of carrying on the work of this commission. I do not believe it is a job for one man; it is not a job for a superintendent of penitentiaries. When the bill was under discussion a year or two ago, I expressed my views on the matter, after studying some of the penitentiaries of this country. At that time I pointed out that if there was to be reform, it must start in other places. It is not my intention to reiterate those opinions to-day but I do make a plea for the men who are in the penal institutions of this country. Give them a chance to learn a trade; give them a chance to be rehabilitated when they leave these institutions. At this time, when great numbers of men will be lost to the country, it is more important than ever before that we attempt this rehabilitation.
So, Mr. Chairman, I say I am pleased that the minister has included in the estimates an amount to provide for the setting up of the commission, and I hope that before long his opinions will find concrete endorsation.
Mr. ADAMSON; When civilians are interned in Canada, do they come under the director of internment operations or under some other body?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They come under the director of internment operations and I have nothing to do with them. They come under the Secretary of State, and under the Minister of National Defence so far as guarding the camps is concerned. The only thing I have to do is to review their appeals when they come to me.

The report of the penitentiary commission was one of the finest reports ever handed down anywhere as far as penal administration is concerned. While I appreciate the argument that at this time of war it might not be practicable to set up the commission as such because of the expenditure that would be involved, I would suggest to the minister that many recommendations that were made by the commission which dealt

with the administration of the various penitentiaries, should be put into effect. Many of those recommendations have not been carried into effect, with the result that there has been a continuing undercurrent of resentment among some of the staffs in penitentiaries at the failure of the government to carry into effect the recommendations made. Would the minister be good enough to outline to the committee what recommendations made, in so far as internal administration in the various penitentiaries is concerned, were in fact carried into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course I have not those documents here. I believe last year I gave to the committee a list of the changes made, and the regulations made following recommendations of the commission.
But since last year, what?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall try to find out, and, let my hon. friend know.

What becomes of all these applications made by the bar association and the police constables' association to the Minister of Justice advocating law reform? I do not wish to criticize the minister, but I have watched his department for many years and it seems to me it suffers because of its failure to follow what a statesman in England said of the Home Office-"the swing of the pendulum in the matter of law reform." Modern reforms have been brought about in England, and have led to the closing of some institutions and a decrease in the cost of the administration of justice.
Dear knows, if ever there was a time we should follow the pendulum, it is now. As I understand it, bills proposed by private members, whether for regulations respecting motor cars, or for some other wise amendments to the statute law, are referred by the department to the attorneys general of the provinces. What have those attorneys general to do with federal law? Under section 91 of the British North America Act the federal parliament has exclusive jurisdiction in matters of this kind. Nevertheless, if any amendment to the law is proposed, it is immediately referred to the attorneys general. Federal power is at a low ebb when that is done, and I say that that power should lead in law reform for all the provinces, if federal power would only assert itself.
I have in my hand a report of a speech made by Mr. Wedgwood, a Labour member in the English House of Commons. Referring to the same principle, and addressing his observations on law reform to the new Home Secretary, he said:

Supply-Justice
One of the difficulties we have to face in this house at the present time is that we no longer change about-the Conservative government five years, the Liberal government five years and the Labour government five years. There is no adequate excuse for any change of policy. Home secretary follows home secretary, not exactly with the same government but with the same general policy of their predecessors, with the result that a policy worked up by the permanent officials becomes more and more powerful. You do not get a rebel going to the home office and saying: "I will change that." He accepts the policy of the officials. In fact, we in this country are getting to a state in which, owing to the absence of the swing of the pendulum, we have a form of papal infallibility. The lord president of the council issues a decree about the internment of all the aliens. A new "pope" comes along, with all the body of the cardinals around him in his office, and checks any tendency to deviate from the rules laid down by his predecessors.
We are getting in the home office the most conservative body of doctrine and officials, all basing themselves on what has been said and done in the past. There is no chance of breaking away.
As I see it, the minister in the Department of Justice must break away from what has been done, or in some other way bring in reforms. Law reform is a very important matter for Canada to-day. I would suggest that the minister be good enough during the recess to consider the suggestions I have indicated and adopt them.

What happens to the funds of organizations declared to be illegal? I have in mind for instance a case of hardship which has been brought about through an organization known as Jehovah's Witnesses. The question as to the advisability of banning or not banning their operations may be considered when we discuss further the motion to set up the committee to consider the defence of Canada regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am
afraid the hon. member will have to wait until the estimates of the Secretary of State are before the committee. I have nothing to do with the point which has been raised. The custodian of enemy property is in charge of those matters.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Have they any money?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Some of them have.

Does the minister mean that in the event of a Canadian citizen in Canada lending money to, let us say, Jehovah's Witnesses, and in the event of the banning of that organization, his money will go to the custodian of enemy property?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As a
trustee, until the war is over, or the matter is disposed of. The money is not confiscated.

I have in mind the case of a man who lent a large sum of money to the organization known as Jehovah's Witnesses. They were paying him back at the rate of so much a month, or on an annuity basis. His entire livelihood is now cut off because he is told that his money is tied up with the custodian of enemy property. All this has come about because he lent his money to an organization which this government decided after the beginning of the war, was illegal. I believe that is most unfair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A situation of that kind would be controlled by the defence of Canada regulations, and they are to be revised by the committee.
I am pleased to have that information from the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No; do
not be in a hurry. We have just begun.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Three
hours on one item!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is
the general item, and debate is always expected on it.

I have not read the report of the penitentiaries commission for some time, but if my memory serves me correctly, there was a recommendation contained therein for the centralization of executions in Canada. In any event, some recommendation of that kind has been made, although I may be wrong when I suggest it was made in the report of the commission.
There is a feeling in many parts of Ontario-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is under provincial jurisdiction.
-that some move should be made toward the centralization of executions in that province. In January of this year we had the first hanging in the county of Peel for the last thirty-five years.
Not enough.

The man who was hanged came from Toronto. In any event, the feelings which are aroused, especially among the children, is something which I believe should be seriously considered. For some days prior to the execution, rumours fly thick and fast, and there is a good deal of talk, particularly among the children, about it. I do not think that sort of thing should be permitted in these days. I would suggest to the Minister of Justice that if anything can be done to centralize executions in Canada, in places
Supply-Justice

where they would not be carried out so publicly, it would be a worthy service to the country at large.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have found out, of course, that that is entirely under provincial jurisdiction. The administration of justice is within the control of the provinces. That is why the matter of law reform, to which the hon. member for Broadview has referred, has not been dealt with more particularly. We enact the criminal law; but criminal trials, criminal courts, sheriffs and matters of that kind are under the control of the provinces.
That applies equally to executions. I have at times received from gentlemen who were applying for the position of hangman in Canada, letters specifying that they were strong and physically able to do the job and were not afraid of carrying out executions. Of course, I had to answer that I had nothing to do with the matter. The sheriff of the district where the execution is to take place is the man who is responsible. He makes arrangements with someone who is known to be an official executioner, and the sheriff takes care to apply immediately to make sure that he will get his man, because if he does not get an executioner he must do the work himself. But this is just to say that we have absolutely nothing to do with that matter.
There is another side to the question raised by my hon. friend. One of the reasons for capital punishment, whatever opinion we may have upon that method, is its deterrent effect upon the community. It has been felt for a long time that it was a good thing that the execution, if an execution had to take place, should be in the very district where the crime had been committed, that its deterrent effect was thereby the greater. I express no opinion myself, but that is the situation behind the state of things which exists to-day.
It may be necessary to have the executions take place in Peel.
I suggest in reciprocation that the central place of execution be Windsor.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is another point of view. W'hen this matter came before the public a few years ago, it was suggested that all executions in the maritime provinces should take place in the town of Dorchester, where the penitentiary is. The people of that community revolted at the idea of their town being made a Golgotha. I think they are right.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.

88.	Remission service, including remuneration to members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force (to be expended under order in council, and not to exceed $1,600) for assistance to this service, and an amount of $10,900 to reimburse the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force the amounts disbursed by them in ordinary pay and allowances to their men on loan to this service, $50,000.
Are applications for remissions dealt with direct by Ottawa, or does the minister have anything to do with the attorneys-general's departments of the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is
dealt with by Ottawa.

In the matter of the reduction or remission of a sentence, does it come direct to and is it dealt with by Ottawa, or does this department have any communication with the provincial attorneys-general's departments before making a decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. We usually ask for a report from the judge who sentenced the man, and from the warden of the penitentiary or the prison, as the case may be, in order to have every particular about the man.

May I ask the minister a question in connection with the mounted police? As a result of the war and some other conditions, in the cities the administration of many federal acts elsewhere administered by the mounted police devolves upon the city police commissions. They are an auxiliary and a helper of that great force. Would it not be possible for the minister to put in the estimates a sum to compensate the municipalities which are doing all this federal work for nothing? The war has placed a big responsibility upon the municipalities. It was intended that the enforcement of all federal law should be on the federal authority, but it is on the provincial attorneys general, who simply delegate it over to the police systems of the country, and the cities have to maintain a large body of men to do federal work. I forget how many statutes apply to the cities, but their enforcement costs a very large sum of money. I think the time has come when there should be some revision of this relationship, whereby our police systems would receive some subsidy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would ask hon. members kindly to wait until the item concerning the mounted police comes up, and I shall have an officer here to supply me with

Supply-Justice
the details. But I must say to my hon. friend that, as far as I can judge, the situation is the other way round. I think the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is doing more to help the provincial and municipal police than the latter are doing in the way of mounted police work.
Would the minister kindly explain what this rather long paragraph of item 88 means, and particularly the latter part of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is the remission service, which is charged with the administration of the Ticket of Leave Act. Applications for tickets of leave come to that branch, and involve a very large amount of work. As far as the last part of the item is concerned, we are employing a few men of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to do some work which was previously being done by regular employees of the department. This we are doing on account of their special qualifications, and we have to reimburse the mounted police in the amount of their salaries.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That covers one part. It is the second item I notice on page 89 of the estimates, where the details are. One is $1,600 for remuneration, the other is for reimbursement. Is there any distinction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. The reimbursement is to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: So is the other. If the minister has not the explanation available, I am not going to pursue the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am unable to say what the distinction is between the item of $1,600 for remuneration and the item of $10,900 for reimbursement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I notice that this $1,600 is to be expended under order in council. I suppose it is just a sum, in special cases, for-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No doubt about that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: While I am on my feet, I might say that this $1,600 must be some special remuneration which is doled out to the mounted police for special services, under order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, for assistance. I am sorry I have not any more information.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Who is the present senior advisory counsel?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is Mr. Gallagher.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: One lawyer in the branch does the whole of the work?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. The present private secretary is an officer of that branch, but actually he is not working there because he is acting as private secretary to the minister. He is a lawyer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Would
the minister say whether in capital cases he reads the evidence himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should like the minister to explain just how careful the department is in capital cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In capital cases, of course, the officers of the branch are very, very careful and particular about that special part of their work. Not only one of the officers under Mr. Gallagher, but Mr. Gallagher himself reads the evidence and he underlines all the parts which ought to be called to the attention of the minister. In cases where it is the recommendation of the officers of the branch that the law should take its course, of course it is the duty of the minister himself to read the evidence and to convince himself that that is the report which should be made to council. When the recommendation is for clemency, I always read the parts of the evidence which are specially brought to my attention, but I do not feel under the same sort of imperative duty to read every word, to look at every comma of the evidence, because the recommendation is that the law should not take its course.
Is this the procedure which is followed also in connection with applications which come to the department for the parolling of prisoners?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
That procedure is followed in connection with applications for parole?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes. Everything comes to the minister after having been considered and studied by the officers of the branch, and after communications having been received from the various persons to whom they have applied for reports, more particularly the judge, sometimes the crown prosecutor, always the warden, as to what the conduct of the prisoner is, and, in some instances, the medical officer when the question arises.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.

I understand there is a vacancy in the king's bench division in New Brunswick through the resignation of the chief justice. As the minister no doubt knows, the chief justice has been ill for a number of years and has not been able to discharge his duties on the bench. Mr. Justice Le Blanc has had other work to do in connection with the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and considerable work has been piling up on the king's bench. May I ask when an appointment will be made? May we expect one soon, and does the minister feel constrained to tell us whom he has in mind for the appointment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is asking a little too much. Perhaps I am doing my bit in the field of economy by waiting before filling the vacancy. There is another vacancy in Canada. There are only two vacancies on the bench, one in New Brunswick and another in Manitoba. I have made investigations and have been informed that the work is not suffering at all. There has been a great decline in litigation in all the provinces, so much so that I was told by the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada that for the first time since the court was established there was, at the last term, not a case from my own province. Therefore litigants are not very active anywhere, and so long as we do not appoint a judge either in New Brunswick or in Manitoba, we have no salary to pay. That is an economy. My hon. friend may be sure that if it appears to me or if I am informed that an appointment is necessary, I shall see to it that one is made. As to who the appointee will be, I respectfully decline to tell my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am not quarrelling with the minister's decision to save the salary of the king's bench judge. May I point out the exact position in New Brunswick. Years ago we had a bench of five or six members-a chief justice, a judge in equity and the others on circuit. They all met and formed a court en banc and no judge sat on appeal from his own decision. Subsequently, about thirty years ago, they decided to change the procedure, and they formed three divisions of the court.

Supply-Justice

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The province did it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes. There was the king's bench, consisting of four judges who did circuit work; there was the chancery division, consisting of the chief justice and two associate justices; the chancery judges formed the appeal division; and in case of an appeal from one of their decisions, the chief justice of the king's bench was called in. Owing to the decline in litigation, the number of appeals has decreased remarkably-there is no doubt about that-and the judges of the chancery division have very little work to do, so little that one of them has been lent to the government in connection with one of the taxation measures passed last year. I am sure he is at the present time doing useful work there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is one of the appeal courts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
He is a
member of the chancery division and the appeal court. With regard to the kings bench division, the chief justice of that division has not heard a case for three years, and he has now resigned. Mr. Justice Le Blanc has in recent years been doing all the work under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, with the result that there have been only two king's bench judges active in the trial of cases; and until very recently I know they were very busy, and in arrears. The whole position in New Brunswick is top-heavy and ought to be rearranged. I quite realize that this is a matter entirely for the province. If they were to create new positions in New Brunswick they would expect this government to make the appointments and pay the salaries of those appointed, I think negotiations ought to be entered into with the government of New Brunswick to effect some permanent, savings there, because the judges on the court of appeal do not have enough to do; make no mistake about that. As a matter of fact, at the last session of that court, opened the other day, there was just one case on the docket. Imagine paying three judges gross salaries of $28,000 a year with a term of the court having just one case! The situation is ridiculous. We are top-heavy.
I think the same thing is in a measure true of the county court bench. There are too many county court judges, six in that little province, drawing $5,000 a year salary and travelling expenses. Here is a case where there could be a substantial saving. I do not suggest that the government should ask the province of New Brunswick to pass legislation eliminating any of the judges now
living; but as these men die or are pensioned off, having arrived at the age of seventy-five, the government might very well reduce the number. That would not be pleasing to some of the boys I know, I do not care what political complexion they are, but it would be a good thing for the taxpayers of Canada. What is true of New Brunswick I fancy is true, perhaps in a lesser degree, of certain other provinces.
I am looking over these estimates and, if I am correct, there are sixty-five county court judges in Ontario. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I
wonder.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It seems
an extraordinary number. Members of the bar from that province may say that some of those county court judges are exceedingly busy. There is no doubt of that, but I suggest that some of them have very little to do. In the interest of national economy in war time, I suggest to the minister that he take this matter up, at least with the province of New Brunswick.

I have

In New

speechtext: I would point out that this discussion has been out of order from the beginning, because the item under consideration is, "Administration, Exchequer Court of Canada," and most of the discussion has been with regard to provincial high courts.

Strictly

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Looking at page 95 of the estimates, I should like some information about pensions to judges. There does not seem to be any particular item under which we can discuss that. I am puzzled to know why Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, who was for many years a distinguished ornament of this house as Minister of Justice, and subsequently chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, should get only $6,666, while Mr. Justice Smith, who was a puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, gets $8,000, and my very learned friend Mr. Justice Mignault gets $12,000. I do not criticize the amounts, but I should like an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When Sir Charles Fitzpatrick retired to become lieutenant-governor of Quebec, he got the superannuation then fixed by law, two-thirds of his salary. The salary then was not what it has become since for the chief justice of the supreme court. In 1921, the salaries of the supreme court judges were increased to $12,000 for the puisne judges, and $15,000 for the chief justice. Then, in 1927 or thereabouts parliament enacted a law retiring the judges of the federal courts, namely, the Supreme Court of Canada and the exchequer court, compulsorily when they reached the age of seventy-five, but it was then enacted that those who had been appointed before this law came into force should retire at that age but with their full salary, because they had been appointed for life at that salary.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should like to point out that under a return brought down here the other day in answer to a question put on the order paper by the - hon. member for York East, Canada is paying this year for superannuation of retired judges, $307,133.30, a rather staggering sum.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. Of course there are the judges both of the Supreme Court of Canada and the exchequer court, and the judges of the various provincial

superior courts. When they are sick or unable to fulfil their duties, they retire with two-thirds of their salary. Then there are the county court judges all over Canada; when they are seventy-five years of age they have the right to retire with their full salary. When they retire because of illness before they are seventy-five years of age, they receive two-thirds of their salary. It does constitute a quite large amount when the total is shown.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is the law, anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it is the law.

The Minister of Justice has just pointed out that there has been a great decrease in the amount of litigation, especially in the Supreme Court of Canada. I notice that the salary of the registrar of the supreme court, which is a recent appointment, has been increased by $1,500. Will the minister please explain that, in view of his own statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the law, the salary of the registrar of the Supreme Court of Canada is fixed by the governor in council and must not exceed $8,000. When the Beatty commission investigated the matter of the higher officers in the civil service, it classified the clerk of the House of Commons, the clerk of the Senate and the registrar of the supreme court together, because each had the rank of deputy minister, and recommended that the salary should be $7,500. Parliament acted accordingly with regard to the clerk of the House of Commons and the clerk of the Senate; their salaries were increased to $7,500, and now the salary of the registrar of the supreme court is placed on the same basis. Of course the registrar sits in chambers, hears motions and carries on a good deal of the procedure of that court; he has a large staff. I could not very well give effect to that recommendation during the last few years because the gentleman who occupied that position, who was a very good registrar, had reached the age where he should have retired, and each year I had to plead with the treasury board to extend his time for another year. In those circumstances I could not very well recommend an increase in salary. I think this is the right thing to do.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There may be something in what the minister has just said as to the reason for increasing this salary, but my recollection is that the Beatty report was made nearly twenty years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Well, long anterior to 1930; I will put it in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

is the date?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: February, 1930.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Very well. In making an appointment after that, the government did not see fit to increase the salary to S7.500. A very competent man was found in the city of Ottawa who was willing to accept this position at $6,000, with free office, free staff, free everything; and I never heard any complaint at all about the work done by the former registrar for $6,000. To me it does seem a little strange that in war time we should increase this salary by 25 per cent. I am going to register a protest against the principle, and I shall have to leave it there.
I wish to point out to the committee and to the country that this is not economy in the normal activity of government in war time.

I should like to support what has just been said by the leader of the opposition. During a time like this, when we are appealing to the people of Canada to make sacrifices and our people are making them, I think it is very difficult to justify an increase of 25 per cent in the salary of the registrar, who last year received S6,000. To me it seems that all these allowances are entirely out of line with what is being received by the great majority of the people of Canada, and I think this amount should be left as it was.

Some months ago, when I saw some criticism with regard to the readjustment of the salary of the registrar of the Supreme Court of Canada, I was very much surprised at the stand taken by some Tory members and especially by the Pickwickian leader of the opposition. Why single out this case, in which there is not an increase but a readjustment of salary, when we see all the promotions that have been made on the recommendation of the civil service commission throughout the various departments? Why single out this case? Is it because the present appointee was formerly a member of the Hepburn government, and the leader of the opposition wants to show his rancour towards Mr. Hepburn by criticizing one of his former colleagues? I wonder whether that is the reason. Why does the hon. gentleman not say something about Tories who have obtained promotions by being transferred from one department to another, men who are pests in some departments and who receive extravagant salaries? I would move that the salary of the leader of the opposition be
reduced to SI. He is just as efficient as the other dollar-a-year men, and he should be treated in the same way. I should like him to tell the committee why he has singled out this case, whether it is to satisfy his rancour against Mr. Hepburn and his government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing in the law about it, but it is a tradition of very long standing that when a judge dies in office, an allowance or gratuity amounting to two months' salary is paid to his widow.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So far as I remember, the auditor general merely calls attention to the discrepancy. He does not suggest a change. As a matter of fact, it is a long standing practice, and was in operation long before I came to the department. Judges of the appeal court in Quebec travel from Quebec to Montreal and from Montreal to Quebec almost continuously. It is an arrangement which went on in years gone by between the chief justice and the Department of Justice whereby, instead of sending their bills for $10 a day, plus transportation expenses, they would be paid $25 for each trip to Montreal or to Quebec. I am told that it works rather to the advantage of the department, and that while the amount is less, the

judges like it better. It is not done strictly under the law, but it is an agreement which has been accepted.

speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The same thing between Victoria and Vancouver.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It grew up, just like Topsy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sorry I cannot give the information. Of course this amount does not need to be voted. It is statutory, and that is the reason why I have not the explanation. I can, however, supply it to my hon. friend at any time.

Under the British North America Act the dominion need pay only the salaries of high court, superior court and county court judges in the provinces. The payment of travelling expenses is an innovation. I doubt whether such payment could be justified under the British North America Act. The travelling expenses must be provided by the provinces for provincial courts and their constitution and administration. They provide the money for the expenses of division court and county court judges. The payment of travelling expenses is an innovation of recent years, and I suggest that the provinces should look after them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
Leader of the Official Opposition
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I was a member of a
select committee of the House of Commons which considered judges' salaries and travelling and other allowances. That committee, which sat a few years ago, was presided over by Senator Duff, and the late W. A. Boys, who at that time was member for Antigonish-Guysborough. It was contended before that committee that allowances for travelling expenses should be paid by the provinces. 
Some of the judges appearing before the committee to present their case showed the cost accounts for the maintenance of their automobiles, and all that sort of thing. That select committee considered the functions of the dominion and the provinces, so far as judges and their expenses were concerned. It was urged that the dominion was obligated to pay only judges' salaries in federal and provincial courts. The Minister of Justice may appoint judges to the superior and county courts, but it is the duty and the function of the provinces to pay any outside allowances.
The board of transport commissioners should have some discretion in the matter. While the government cannot afford to pay a few dollars to carry the soldiers, yet it can afford over $2,000,000 for salaries and travelling allowances of judges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Travelling expenses of judges of the superior and county courts, in carrying out the work of those courts, have to be paid by the federal parliament. In some provinces, judges of the county courts do outside work for the provinces. Even at this very session of the Ontario legislature a bill is being placed before the house for the purpose of paying travelling expenses of county court judges who may do provincial work outside the county court seats. We have declined to pay travelling expenses of judges who do that sort of work.
It was a matter of some controversy in the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Would the minister explain the procedure in the event of a county court judgeship becoming vacant? In my constituency the county court judge died a few years ago, and since that time no appointment has been made. On March 2, 1939, I made some remarks on the establishment of the proposed penitentiaries commission, which remarks will be found at pages 1478-1481 of

Supply-Justice

Hansard of that session. I still maintain the same view that I then expressed, that the Minister of Justice himself can look after the penitentiaries better than any commission. He has done so in the past for a great many years and I have every confidence in him.
I do not see the necessity for any such commission; besides that, I have always been opposed to the establishment of managing or administrative commissions, and this would be one of them. The result of the work of most investigating commissions is to suggest the creation of an administrative commission, and once these administrative commissions are set up it is very difficult for members of the house to get information with regard to their work. That is the case with the broadcasting corporation, for example. I am therefore opposed to this proposed commission.
I am opposed to it also because I am interested in the welfare of the prisoners in the penitentiaries, provided that one is not too lenient with them, for, of course, when they are condemned by a court, it is not because of the good actions they have done. On the other hand, they are entitled to justice. The fact of their being condemned to the penitentiary does not deprive them of their citizenship or change them from being human beings. We must therefore see to it that they are treated fairly. Moreover, we should try to make good citizens out of them.
The way to keep control over the administration of our penitentiaries is to leave parliament free to inquire into their management. We can do so when the minister is head of the penitentiaries, but if that work was delegated to a commission it would be most difficult for members of the house to get any information about the penitentiaries. I do aot say that to contradict our respected and beloved Minister of Justice. I say it because I believe it and because also in the Liberal party we have the right to express our views freely. We are not rubber stamps, as the leader of the opposition very improperly suggested the other day in quite an offensive way. I do not know what member of the house or of this committee would call Jean-Frangois Pouliot a rubber stamp. Is he not a good Liberal? Once more the leader of the opposition was all wrong.
I hope the minister will take into consideration the views I have expressed. I remember that last year one of the bright members for Vancouver, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green)-he sits on the other side of the house but he is bright nevertheless- suggested that appointments should be made to the proposed penitentiaries commission. I fought against that. A year has since passed and no commission has been appointed, and I thank the minister from the bottom of my
